summary: Presents a functional description of the protocol extensions needed to support recovery in GMPLS, that is, protection and restoration. Protocol-specific formats and mechanisms are described in companion documents. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: When part of a network breaks, traffic should switch to a backup path. This describes what protocols must do to make that happen.

questions: gmpls span protection vs end-to-end protection
subtitle: How GMPLS networks detect a failed link or path and move traffic onto a backup, described as abstract steps and messages.

tldr.problem: Optical and electronic switching equipment sharing a common control plane needs signaling, routing and link management that support recovery from data plane faults.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes span protection (1+1, 1:1 and shared M:N) and end-to-end protection and restoration as sequences of abstract messages such as Failure Indication, Switchover Request and Switchover Response.
tldr.outcome: It is a functional description only: message formats and encodings are left to companion documents. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 4426 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2006, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. Its terminology comes from RFC 4427.

sections.title: Recovery in GMPLS
sections.content:
A common control plane for optical and electronic switching equipment needs signaling, routing and link management mechanisms that support data plane fault recovery. The RFC uses recovery to mean both protection and restoration, and the two terms are told apart by the resource allocation done during the recovery period (see RFC 4427).

A label-switched path (LSP) can be recovered at three levels: local span protection (the link between two neighboring switches), segment protection (a piece of the LSP between two boundary nodes) and end-to-end protection (the whole LSP from ingress to egress). Several levels can be used at once, but a switch in one direction of the LSP results in both directions being switched to a new span, segment or end-to-end path.

The document is purely functional. Protocol-specific formats, encoding and mechanisms are left to companion documents.
sections.eli5: A path through the network can be saved in small pieces, in bigger pieces, or all at once. This RFC explains what the network has to say to itself to do that.

sections.title: Span Protection Models
sections.content:
Span protection guards one link between two neighboring nodes, A and B. Under 1+1 protection a dedicated link j is pre-assigned to protect working link i. Traffic is permanently bridged onto both links and the receiving node picks one, for example by signal quality. In the unidirectional variant, each node chooses on its own, so A may receive from link i while B receives from link j. In the bi-directional variant the nodes coordinate so both use the same link, which needs a Switchover Request message sent reliably to the other node, and a Switchover Response in return.

Under 1:1 protection the dedicated protection link may carry pre-emptable Extra Traffic. One node is the master and the other the slave. If the slave sees the failure, it tells the master with a failure indication. The master allocates the protection link, asks the slave to switch, and the slave acknowledges. Extra Traffic is dropped before the switch, which drops more traffic than needed but is preferred over possible misconnections.

Under shared M:N protection a set of N working links is protected by a set of M protection links, usually with M =< N. The master applies policy and picks which protection link to use. Which working links get restored when protection links run short is left to policies the RFC does not specify.

Each model needs three things: routing announces one TE link with a Link Protection Type (such as Dedicated 1+1, Dedicated 1:1 or Shared M:N), signaling SHOULD carry the Link Protection object, and both nodes MUST agree on the protection association, via LMP or manual configuration.
sections.eli5: Imagine two towns joined by a main road and a spare road. Both towns must agree when to start using the spare road, and one town is in charge of choosing.

sections.title: Span Protection Messages
sections.content:
Three abstract messages are used in local span protection. They SHOULD be delivered reliably, with sequencing, acknowledgement and retransmission. Their format and encoding are given elsewhere.

  • Failure Indication: sent from slave to master, listing one or more failed working links. It may not be needed when the transport technology already provides notification. A node may split failures across several messages to meet its own time limits.
  • Switchover Request: under bi-directional 1+1 it coordinates the selecting function at both nodes. Under 1:1 and M:N the master sends it to the slave to say the LSPs on the failed link can move to a named protection link, with LSP labels if needed. One failure indication can lead to several requests.
  • Switchover Response: sent from slave to master to report that the switchover is complete or failed. On failure, both nodes notify the operator.

Where link bundling is used and labels are the same on working and protection links, LSPs may be moved without re-signaling each one.
sections.eli5: There are three little notes: "something broke", "please switch to the spare", and "done" or "I could not". They must not get lost on the way.

sections.title: End-to-End Protection and Restoration
sections.content:
End-to-end recovery moves an entire LSP from initiator to terminator. The RFC covers three previously proposed schemes.

In unidirectional 1+1, a dedicated, resource-disjoint alternate path is pre-established and traffic is sent on both paths. The end nodes receive from whichever works, and there is no explicit signaling. In bi-directional 1+1 the end nodes must coordinate. A node on the working path that detects a failure MUST send a Failure Indication toward an end node, or the end nodes detect it themselves. An end node that sees the failure starts receiving from the protection path and sends a Switchover Request. The other end does the same and replies with a Switchover Response.

In shared mesh restoration, protection paths for several LSPs share link and node resources. Capacity is pre-reserved, but explicit signaling along the protection path is needed to activate a protection LSP. Sharing is typically limited to LSPs whose working paths are physically diverse. It is designed for a single failure, and with concurrent failures the protection path can be activated for at most one of the LSPs claiming it.

Each node on the working or protection path MUST know the LSP identifier, and the end points MUST associate the working and protection paths until the LSP is de-provisioned. Failure Indication messages MUST be sent reliably and need not follow the failed LSP's path.
sections.eli5: Instead of fixing one block of a road, you plan a whole second route from start to finish. Sometimes many drivers share one spare route, because it is unlikely everyone's main route breaks at once.

sections.title: Reversion and Priorities
sections.content:
Reversion means moving an LSP back to the original working path after the fault is repaired. It is desired because the protection path may be less optimal and because it frees protection resources for other LSPs. Its disadvantage is a second service disruption, and use is at the operator's option. A "bridge-and-switch" (make-before-break) approach minimizes disruption: the source bridges traffic onto both paths, sends a Bridge and Switch Request, the destination answers with a Bridge and Switch Response, and the source finishes with a Bridge and Switch Completed message so the protection path can be de-activated.

Other administrative procedures include forcing a switchover and locking out switchover, and these have to be supported by signaling.

When a failure hits more than one working link and there are too few protection links, the decision about what to protect MAY be based on LSP priorities. Failures may also be detected one after another, so a later failure of higher-priority LSPs may bump LSPs already switched over.
sections.eli5: Once the main road is fixed you may want to move back, but doing it carefully so cars are not stopped twice. Important cars get the spare lane first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The messages can face interception, spoofing, modification and replay. Signaling MUST be able to provide authentication, integrity and protection against replay attacks. Privacy and confidentiality are not required, and protecting the identity of data plane end points in Failure Indication messages is not required.

The RFC warns that false Failure Indication messages, or tampered LSP identifiers, can trigger unneeded recovery actions, desynchronize the control and data planes and raise the risk of misconnections. When Extra Traffic is involved, the wrong traffic could easily reach the wrong destination. An intruder could also set up what looks like a valid protection LSP and then cause a fault to divert traffic. Mechanisms used to secure routing information exchange SHOULD be applied too.
sections.eli5: If a stranger can shout "the road is closed!", they can send everyone the wrong way. So the notes must be checked to make sure they are real.

messages.note: Sent if the slave detects the failure.

messages.label: Switchover Request
messages.note: Names the protection link to use.
